title: Biplanar Videoradiography to Study the Wrist and Distal Radioulnar Joints
protocol: Prepare the specimens or subjects for the CT scan.
Acquire a CT scan of the distal forearm with a 25 cm data collection diameter.
Reconstruct the images with a 20 cm field-of-view using the Bone Plus convolution algorithm.
Use tube settings of 80 kVp and 80 mA for the CT scan.
Limit the forearm exposure to approximately 7 cm proximal of the distal radius surface to the distal phalanges.
Transfer the acquired CT images to the laboratory's computer in DICOM format.
Position the image intensifiers below the forearms.
Set the angle between the image intensifiers at 110°.
Aim the X-ray sources downward to the corresponding IIs at a 55° orientation relative to the ground.
Generate X-rays in continuous mode with an exposure setting between 65 to 75 kV.
Adjust the source-to-image distances of both X-Ray-II pairs to approximately 130 cm.
Set the source-to-hand distances at 90 cm.
Place a trestle or similar structure between the image intensifiers for item placement.
Place undistortion grids onto the imaging intensifiers and capture their images both before and after videoradiography data.
Save undistortion grid images as 8-bit TIFF images for both X-ray sources.
Capture radiographs of the calibration cube in various orientations 4 times before performing the experiment.
Capture radiographs of the calibration cube in various orientations 4 times after the experiment to confirm setup stability throughout the experiment.
Save all calibration cube images as 8-bit TIFF images for both X-ray sources.
Define tasks to capture wrist motion during flexion-extension, radial-ulnar deviation, and circumduction.
Describe distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) motion tasks as forearm rotation from a holding pose to full pronation or supination.
Acquire videoradiographs of the wrist at its neutral pose with the back of the hand coplanar with the back of the forearm.
Set up camera for videoradiograph acquisition at 200 Hz and shutter speed of 500 µs.
Record two seconds of imaging for each task to acquire 2 repetitions.
Anonymize the DICOMs and import them into image processing software for 3D modeling (e.g., Mimics Materialise).
Open the Anonymize window from the File toolbar in Mimics Materialise software.
Select Anonymize All Images from the left tab.
Press the Anonymize button on the bottom right.
Segment the bones or implants of interest using a previously described methodology.
Select the Threshold option from the Segment toolbar and choose predefined threshold sets for Bone when the window is opened.
Create the thresholded mask, then use the Split Mask option to manually paint regions of bones or implant's components.
Click OK after all regions are colored; wait for the software to generate masks for each bone and implant component automatically.
Check all generated masks to ensure they cover intended regions completely.
Use the Edit Masks option to modify regions manually if necessary.
For studying the wrist joint, segment and separate the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals and radius bones from the rest of bones.
Optionally, segment the capitate and other bones for post-processing stages.
For studying the DRUJ, segment and separate the radius and ulna from the rest of bones.
For implants, segment the radial component and the carpal component with its screws.
Use a CAD model or 3D surface scanner to generate the 3D model of the explanted radial component.
Register the generated 3D model to the rough segmentation of the radial component using Mimics Materialise default’s method.
Generate a full-mask of the image volume containing all grey values by selecting the Threshold option from the Segment toolbar.
Adjust the threshold values from the minimum to the maximum grey-values.
Use the Boolean Operators option and subtract the segmented volume of the bone or implant of interest from the generated full-mask.
Change the color of this partial volume's mask to black (RGB: 0.0/0.0/0.0).
Export the mask as a DICOM file by selecting Export DICOM… in the software.
Convert the segmented masks to triangulated meshed 3D surface models.
Select the Calculate 3D option with Optimal Resolution.
Export the 3D models in VRML format.
Import undistortion grid images and calibration images for each subject in XMALab software.
Create a new trial in XMALab software.
Assign folder paths to Undistortion Grid images and calibration images.
Click the Compute Undistortion button to de-distort radiographs.
Detect the centers of all holes by the software.
Change the workspace to Calibration workspace.
Determine the calibration matrices using XMALab software.
Model X-ray sources as pinhole cameras with intrinsic and extrinsic parameters in XMALab.
Select each of the 4 reference items (Pyramid, Jack, Dome, Helix) placed in the calibration cube for all sets of images and for each view.
Press Compute Calibration if the points are not automatically found by the software.
Optimize Camera Setup after all calibration images have been calibrated.
Export calibration matrices after optimization.
Sort through all 8 calibration sets to find the set with the smallest error undistorted.
Press the information option in the top-right corner of each calibration window to determine the lowest error value.
Select the image with the lowest error and export it using the MayaCams 2.0 option from the File-Export menu.
Change the workspace to Marker tracking.
Load the videoradiographs captured in CINE-format by pressing the + icon.
After loading, export the undistorted trial images by selecting Undistorted Trial Images from the File-Export menu.
Enhance image features using filters for accurate model-based tracking.
Define parameters of contrast (intensity detection), Sobel (edge detection), Gaussian (blurring/smoother), and Sharpen (boldening edges).
Select the Rad Renderer or DRR Renderer objects shown in the top-left widget to apply the defined filters.
Press C or click on Track Current button from the toolbar to find the best match between the DRR and the radiographs.
Use the normalized cross-correlation (NCC) cost function for matching.
Execute optimization via the Tracking Dialog by pressing the Tracking Dialog option from the toolbar.
In the new window, change From Frame and To Frame to 0, then press OK.
Open the Tracking Dialog after the first frame is automatically optimized.
Change the From Frame to 0 and set the To Frame to the last frame number in the sequence.
Use the particle swarm optimization (PSO) method within a region of 3 mm and 3° for the optimization process.
Check all frames manually to ensure the optimization has been executed correctly.
Repeat the steps described in section 2.3.2 and 2.3.3 if DRR and radiographs are not matched correctly.
Track the wrist using a model that includes the second and third metacarpals (MC2-MC3) to reduce bone overlap effects.
Transform the matched and optimized MC2-MC3 locations to the MC3 partial image volume.
Seed initial positions of the MC3 for tracking based on transformed locations.
Track the MC3 using the seeded positions.
Track the radius, ulna, radial component, and carpal component in videoradiographs during all tasks.
Based on the provided protocol, here are the formatted experimental steps:
Define ulnar variance as the distance between the ulnar fovea and the sigmoid notch on the radius.
Calculate contact patterns between the polyethylene cap and radial component using wrist kinematics and component-specific distance fields.
Calculate distance fields for each 3D surface model as a volumetric array of signed distances from the surface.
Calculate proximity values on the surface of the polyethylene cap and radial component for each posture.
Adjust these proximity values to the resolution of the acquisition system (distance exclusion threshold was selected as 0.70 mm).
Use Bland-Altman analysis to evaluate accuracy by demonstrating bias and 95% limit of agreement between BVR and OMC.
Describe the center of rotation behavior of the healthy wrist using generalized linear models.
Find a relationship between the change in UV and PS (UV = p1×PS2 + p2×PS) using coefficients optimized with linear regression.
Evaluate the model's accuracy using the root-mean-squared-error metric.
